nameStory: The 'rattlesnake plantain' name comes from the distinctive white markings on the dark green leaves that look remarkably like the patterned scales of a rattlesnake's skin. Despite the scary name, this beautiful orchid was actually believed by some to be a remedy for snakebites - though we definitely don't recommend testing that theory! The 'western' part distinguishes it from its eastern cousins, though it does appear rarely in parts of New England.
description: Western rattlesnake plantain is a ground-hugging orchid that forms rosettes of broad, oval-shaped leaves marked with striking white veins. The leaves grow 2-4 inches long and lie flat against the forest floor in attractive patches. In summer, it sends up a single flower stalk up to a foot tall, topped with small white orchid flowers that may spiral around the stem or all face the same direction. This is one of our most distinctive woodland orchids, even when not in bloom.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad oval leaves arranged in a flat rosette, dark green with a prominent white stripe down the center and often delicate white net-like veining throughout - the snakeskin pattern that gives this plant its name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white orchid flowers clustered along the top portion of an upright stem, each flower having the characteristic orchid shape with a pouched lip - they may spiral around the stalk or all lean to one side

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms patches of ground-level leaf rosettes connected by underground runners, with individual flower stalks rising 6-12 inches above the leaves in summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel thick and somewhat succulent to the touch, with a smooth, waxy surface that makes the white veining stand out dramatically against the dark background

habitat: In New England, this rare orchid is found in cool, moist coniferous or mixed forests, often in the understory of spruce, fir, or hemlock. It prefers acidic, humus-rich soil and is most likely to be encountered in northern New England's mountain forests. Look for it in shaded areas with consistent moisture and good leaf litter.

seasonality.spring: Evergreen leaves are most noticeable as snow melts, showing their distinctive white-veined pattern against the dark forest floor. New growth may begin to emerge from the center of established rosettes.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in mid to late summer, with the distinctive white orchid blooms appearing on tall stalks above the leaf rosettes. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules may develop, while the patterned leaves remain prominent and easy to spot among fallen autumn leaves.
seasonality.winter: The thick, evergreen leaves persist under snow cover, though they may appear somewhat dulled - still identifiable by their distinctive white markings if uncovered.

funFact: This orchid is incredibly rare in New England with only 6 recorded observations - you're more likely to see an actual rattlesnake than this 'rattlesnake' plant! It's much more common in the western mountains where it earned its name, making any New England sighting a truly special botanical discovery.
confusionNotes: The white-veined leaves make this species unmistakable among New England's rattlesnake plantains - the other species have either fuzzy white veining (downy rattlesnake plantain) or a checkerboard pattern (checkered rattlesnake plantain). Remember: bold white center stripe plus net veining equals western rattlesnake plantain.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'western,' this species does occasionally appear in northern New England and the Great Lakes region, likely remnants from when cooler climates extended further south. The extreme rarity in our region makes every sighting scientifically valuable - if you find one, consider reporting it to local botanists or iNaturalist.
compareHints: Western rattlesnake plantain has the boldest white markings of all our rattlesnake plantains, with a prominent white center stripe and clear net veining. Downy rattlesnake plantain has softer, more diffuse white veining, while checkered rattlesnake plantain shows a distinct checkerboard pattern rather than net-like veins. Lesser rattlesnake plantain is much smaller overall with more subtle markings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Downy rattlesnake plantain is the most common of the three rattlesnake plantains in New England.
Among rattlesnake plantains, checkered rattlesnake plantain has the most pronounced white reticulated veining creating distinct geometric patterns across the entire leaf surface.
Lesser rattlesnake plantain is distinguished from downy rattlesnake plantain by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance.
